# Numerical Algorithm for the Dirichlet Problem and Energy Minimization

## Problem Restatement

We seek a function $\phi$ satisfying

$$\nabla^2 \phi = 0 \quad \text{in } \mathcal{R}, \qquad \phi\big|_{\partial\mathcal{R}} = g,$$

and we want (a) a numerical algorithm to compute $\phi$, and (b) an explanation of why that algorithm simultaneously minimizes the Dirichlet energy

$$E[\phi] \;=\; \iiint_{\mathcal{R}} \|\nabla \phi\|^2 \, dV.$$

---

## Part 1. The Relaxation (Finite-Difference) Algorithm

### 1.1 Discretization

Cover $\mathcal{R}$ with a regular grid of spacing $h$ (in 2D for clarity; the 3D case is identical with two extra neighbors). Label interior grid points by $(i,j)$ with $\phi_{i,j} \approx \phi(x_i, y_j)$.

The standard 5-point (2D) / 7-point (3D) finite-difference approximation of the Laplacian is

$$\nabla^2 \phi \;\approx\; \frac{1}{h^2}\Big(\phi_{i+1,j}+\phi_{i-1,j}+\phi_{i,j+1}+\phi_{i,j-1}-4\phi_{i,j}\Big).$$

Setting $\nabla^2\phi = 0$ gives the **discrete mean-value property**:

$$\boxed{\;\phi_{i,j} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{4}\big(\phi_{i+1,j}+\phi_{i-1,j}+\phi_{i,j+1}+\phi_{i,j-1}\big)\;} \tag{1}$$

(3D: average of 6 neighbors with coefficient $1/6$.)

### 1.2 Boundary conditions

For every grid node lying on (or nearest) $\partial\mathcal{R}$, fix $\phi_{i,j} = g(x_i,y_j)$. These values never change.

### 1.3 Iterative relaxation

Equation (1) is a large sparse linear system $A\boldsymbol{\phi} = \boldsymbol{b}$. Rather than inverting $A$ directly, we solve it iteratively:

- **Jacobi:** update every interior point simultaneously using (1) with the previous iterate's values.
- **Gauss–Seidel (successive displacement):** update points one at a time, using already-updated neighbors immediately. This is the classical **"relaxation method"** of Southwell.
- **Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR):** extrapolate each Gauss–Seidel correction by a factor $\omega\in(1,2)$:
$$\phi_{i,j}^{(n+1)} = \phi_{i,j}^{(n)} + \omega\Big[\tfrac14(\phi_{i+1,j}+\phi_{i-1,j}+\phi_{i,j+1}+\phi_{i,j-1})-\phi_{i,j}^{(n)}\Big].$$

SOR with optimal $\omega^* = 2/(1+\sin(\pi h/L))$ reduces the iteration count from $O(N^2)$ (Gauss–Seidel) to $O(N)$ for an $N\times N$ grid.

**Convergence:** The iteration matrix of Gauss–Seidel/Jacobi has spectral radius $<1$ for the discrete Laplacian with Dirichlet boundary data (the matrix is strictly diagonally dominant and an M-matrix), so the iteration converges to the unique solution of $A\boldsymbol{\phi}=\boldsymbol{b}$ for any initial guess.

This is the complete numerical algorithm: **discretize → fix boundary → iterate the local averaging rule (1) until convergence.**

---

## Part 2. Why the Algorithm Minimizes the Energy

### 2.1 The Dirichlet principle (continuous case)

Define the quadratic energy functional

$$E[u] \;=\; \iiint_{\mathcal{R}} \|\nabla u\|^2\, dV.$$

Its first variation is, for any admissible variation $v$ with $v|_{\partial\mathcal{R}}=0$,

$$\delta E[u; v] \;=\; 2\iiint_{\mathcal{R}} \nabla u\cdot \nabla v \, dV \;=\; -2\iiint_{\mathcal{R}} v\,\nabla^2 u\, dV \;+\; 2\oint_{\partial\mathcal{R}} v\,\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\, dS.$$

The boundary term vanishes because $v|_{\partial\mathcal{R}}=0$. Hence

$$\delta E[u; v] = 0 \;\forall v \;\iff\; \nabla^2 u = 0 \text{ in } \mathcal{R}.$$

Since $E$ is convex (its second variation $2\iiint\|\nabla v\|^2 dV \ge 0$), this stationary point is the **unique global minimizer** among all functions agreeing with $g$ on $\partial\mathcal{R}$. This is the **Dirichlet principle**: the harmonic function is exactly the energy minimizer.

### 2.2 The discrete energy and its gradient

On the grid, define the **discrete Dirichlet energy**

$$E_h[\boldsymbol{\phi}] \;=\; \sum_{\text{edges }(p,q)} \big(\phi_p - \phi_q\big)^2. \tag{2}$$

(Up to the constant factor $h^{d-2}$ this is the discrete analogue of $\iiint\|\nabla\phi\|^2 dV$; the constant does not affect the minimizer.)

The partial derivative with respect to one interior node $\phi_{i,j}$ is

$$\frac{\partial E_h}{\partial \phi_{i,j}} \;=\; 2\sum_{q\sim (i,j)}\big(\phi_{i,j}-\phi_q\big) \;=\; 2\Big[4\phi_{i,j}-\phi_{i+1,j}-\phi_{i-1,j}-\phi_{i,j+1}-\phi_{i,j-1}\Big]. \tag{3}$$

Setting (3) to zero reproduces **exactly** the mean-value rule (1). Therefore:

> **The discrete Laplace equation (1) is precisely the Euler–Lagrange (stationarity) condition of the discrete energy (2).**

Because $E_h$ is a positive-semidefinite quadratic form (a sum of squares), it is strictly convex in the interior variables, so the stationary point is the **unique global minimizer**.

### 2.3 The relaxation step *is* gradient descent on $E_h$

From (3), the Gauss–Seidel update can be rewritten as

$$\phi_{i,j}^{(n+1)} \;=\; \phi_{i,j}^{(n)} \;-\; \frac{1}{8}\,\frac{\partial E_h}{\partial \phi_{i,j}}\Big|_{\text{using latest neighbors}}. \tag{4}$$

So each relaxation sweep is a **coordinate descent** (exact line search along one coordinate) on the discrete energy $E_h$:

- Jacobi = simultaneous gradient step with step size $1/8$.
- Gauss–Seidel = cyclic coordinate descent.
- SOR = over-relaxed coordinate descent.

Because $E_h$ is convex and bounded below, coordinate descent converges to the unique minimizer. Thus:

> **The numerical relaxation algorithm does not merely "solve a linear system" — it is literally a descent method that monotonically reduces the discrete energy $E_h$ at every step, and its fixed point is the global minimizer of $E_h$.**

One can verify monotonicity directly: replacing $\phi_{i,j}$ by the average of its neighbors is the value that minimizes the sum of the four edge-squared-differences incident to $(i,j)$ holding the neighbors fixed, so $E_h$ cannot increase under a Gauss–Seidel sweep.

---

## Part 3. Summary

| Element | Continuous | Discrete / Numerical |
|---|---|---|
| Unknown | $\phi$, $\nabla^2\phi=0$ | $\phi_{i,j}$, mean-value rule (1) |
| Energy | $E[\phi]=\iiint\|\nabla\phi\|^2 dV$ | $E_h=\sum_{\text{edges}}(\phi_p-\phi_q)^2$ |
| Stationarity | $\delta E=0 \iff \nabla^2\phi=0$ | $\partial E_h/\partial\phi_{i,j}=0 \iff$ rule (1) |
| Algorithm | — (analytic) | Relaxation: iterate (1) with fixed boundary |
| Mechanism | Dirichlet principle | Coordinate descent on $E_h$, eq. (4) |

**The numerical algorithm** is the **finite-difference relaxation method**: discretize $\mathcal{R}$ on a grid, impose the boundary values $g$ on boundary nodes, and iteratively replace each interior value by the average of its neighbors (Jacobi / Gauss–Seidel / SOR) until convergence.

**It minimizes the energy** because the discrete averaging rule is exactly the vanishing-gradient condition of the discrete Dirichlet energy $E_h$, and each relaxation update is a coordinate-descent step that strictly decreases $E_h$; convexity of $E_h$ guarantees the iterates converge to its unique global minimizer — the discrete harmonic function, which is the discrete analogue of the continuous energy minimizer guaranteed by the Dirichlet principle.

### PROOF COMPLETE
